To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
unsupervised text categorization can be performed by learning from neighbors in the representation vector space.

(i) unsupervised text classifiers based on nearest neighbors are a promising direction for unsupervised text analysis; (ii) DocSCAN is the first method to achieve this goal; (iii) DocSCAN outperforms all unsupervised baselins on five text classification benchmarks; and (iv) DocSCAN achieves performance comparable to supervised methods on datasets with relatively few classes.
DocSCAN, a novel approach to unsupervised text clustering based on semantic representations, outperforms various baselines on a range of topic classification datasets.
In summary, our research is concerned with
unsupervised text categorization and the use of language models for this purpose.
the following question: can we use unsupervised learning to achieve the performance of supervised models?
a fundamental question: can unsupervised learning be used to solve a wide range of classification tasks, without relying on human labels?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
DocSCAN is a promising unsupervised approach for classification of documents, but it is not the silver bullet.
the proposed approach, DocSCAN, is the state of the art in unsupervised text categorization, and it outperforms the best unsupervised baseline by a wide margin.
DocSCAN is a powerful and flexible unsupervised classification approach that works well for a wide variety of classification problems, but not for all of them.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
unsupervised classification is possible for text, but not for images.
unsupervised text categorization is a viable approach in many scenarios, but it has its limits.
DocSCAN can be a useful alternative to supervised text classification in cases when labels are not available, but a large unlabeled dataset can be accessed.
The main takeaway from our work is that
unsupervised learning of document topics is feasible, even in the absence of ground-truth labels.
unsupervised classification is a viable and competitive alternative to supervised approaches in many scenarios.
unsupervised learning of text representations is not enough for classification tasks, and that the use of weak supervision signals can improve classification results significantly.
